source.title: To grok or not to grok: Disentangling generalization and memorization on corrupted algorithmic datasets
source.authors: Darshil Doshi; Aritra Das; Tian-Yu He; Andrey Gromov

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The supplied text is a conference paper published at ICLR 2024.
record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization and generalization under label corruption on modular arithmetic datasets, rather than random image labels; it also studies how regularization changes those outcomes.
record.gate_note: Results on noisy modular-arithmetic labels bear on the corruption and regularization versions. The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) on fitting random labels; that cited result is not extracted as this study's result. It does not test shuffled pixels, independent pixel permutations, Gaussian-noise inputs, or learning real and random labels in sequence.
record.test_reason: The study measures training and test accuracy under random label corruption in modular arithmetic and MNIST, testing V4 and parts of V5 in these settings. It does not test completely random labeling as required by V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct: memorization and generalization can coexist, and regularization can suppress corrupted-label memorization through distinct mechanisms. Qualify its scope: the main mechanistic analysis uses interpretable modular-arithmetic models, but the paper also experiments with Transformers, deeper ReLU MLPs and MNIST. Regularization does not uniformly produce inversion across architectures.
record.recipe_differences: Uses two-layer MLPs and other architectures on modular arithmetic and MNIST with symmetric label corruption; it does not reproduce the original random-label image experiments. The paper states full-batch AdamW and MSE as the default, with other settings noted for particular experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome changes with corruption fraction, training data fraction, weight decay, Dropout, BatchNorm, batch size, architecture, activation, loss, and optimizer; the text gives qualitative phase changes for many settings.

fits_no_version.finding: BatchNorm weights correlate with neuronal IPR while low-IPR neurons persist.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BatchNorm can suppress memorizing neurons' contributions without removing their representations.

record.problems: The authors state that the study is limited to exactly solvable models and algorithmic datasets. Many phase-diagram outcomes are presented graphically and described qualitatively rather than with per-condition numeric accuracies. The text says training dynamics leading to the solutions remains an open question.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying result rows were omitted. Several figures report phase diagrams without recoverable per-condition numeric values; the text's qualitative results are captured in the relevant rows rather than transcribing figure-only points.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling and its comparison with true-label training using unchanged architecture and hyperparameters; the stated corruption sweep ends at 0.9.
Training-time ratios for true versus random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The fully corrupted endpoint and a quantitatively established steady test-error trajectory over the complete corruption range.
Fitting completely random labels under regularization, data augmentation, and a controlled removal-of-regularization comparison on true labels. The reported tests concern partially corrupted labels.
Direct comparison of when shared real-data patterns and individual noisy labels are learned. Train/test grokking curves do not separately measure their acquisition.

missing.what: Partial inversion occurs without any explicit regularization when training data are ample. R1 captures only unregularized coexistence.

Mini-batch training without explicit regularization produces partial and full inversion; decreasing batch size enhances inversion. This qualifies perfect training fit even without explicit regularization.
missing.locator: Section 2.1; Appendix F, Figure 10; Appendix J, Figure 22

missing.what: Cross-entropy training requires stronger regularization than MSE; inversion occurs in a narrow weight-decay band, and dropout must be very high to attain inversion.
Two-layer ReLU networks require stronger regularization for grokking than quadratic networks, and moderate dropout can produce confusion.
Modular multiplication reproduces the coexistence, inversion, memorization and forgetting phase structure under weight decay.

record.verdict_notes: Randomly corrupting training labels is the experimental manipulation relevant to this phenomenon, so it does not by itself disqualify the study. Partial corruption must nevertheless remain distinct from V1's completely random labeling. Phase names use coarse accuracy thresholds; they should not be converted into exact accuracies for every plotted condition. Grokking's delayed test accuracy does not establish that noisy labels were learned before shared patterns.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test completely random labels (the corruption sweep reaches ξ = 0.9, not 1.0), image datasets, or whether the same architecture and training hyperparameters fit true and completely random labels.
No comparison of training time or convergence slowdown across corruption fractions is reported.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.

The study tests symmetric random label corruption on modular arithmetic, but does not establish a steadily rising test error from none to all corruption while training accuracy remains perfect across the sweep.
Tests regularization effects on corrupted modular-arithmetic labels. Does not establish that removing regularization alone makes true-label generalization poor.
Does not test whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, or compare their learning dynamics over training.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network with quadratic activation function, width N = 500
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with symmetric random label corruption; no explicit regularization.
rows.value: Both train and test accuracies are close to 100% despite label corruption.
rows.note: The paper calls this Coexistence. This is partial-corruption modular arithmetic, not a completely random labeling.
rows.check: Near-perfect fitting and generalization are reported at 35% corruption without regularization. Remove V1: labels are not completely random. This single condition does not establish V4's degradation curve.

source_check.correct: V4: perfect fitting is observed, but this condition does not establish steadily increasing test error; the complete V4 effect cannot be determined from this row. V5: useful generalization without explicit regularization is observed on partially corrupted data.
source_check.problem: A single observed state overstates evidence for the complete V4 claim.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network with quadratic activation function, width N = 500
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with symmetric random label corruption and weight decay.
rows.value: Generalizes on test data but only memorizes a fraction of corrupted training data; predicts the true labels on the remaining corrupted examples.
rows.note: The paper calls this Partial Inversion. It reports test accuracy near 100% and training accuracy below 100%.
rows.check: Only some corrupted labels are memorized at weight decay 5; training fit is incomplete. Remove V1.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2, Partial Inversion; Figure 1(b); Appendix A.1.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network with quadratic activation function, width N = 500
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with symmetric random label corruption and weight decay.
rows.value: Test accuracy is 100%; training accuracy plateaus close to 100(1 − ξ)%; the model does not memorize any corrupted examples.
rows.note: The paper calls this Full Inversion. Generalization is high, while corrupted training labels are not memorized.
rows.check: Corrupted-label memorization is absent at weight decay 15, rather than merely partial. Training accuracy is approximately 65% while test accuracy reaches 100%. Remove V1.

conditions.value: very high label corruption and/or very low training data-fraction

rows.value: Close to 100% accuracy on training data, but random guessing accuracy on test data.
rows.note: The description specifies memorization of corrupted and uncorrupted training examples. It does not name exact values of corruption or data fraction for this result.
rows.check: The textual phase description reports near-perfect training fit and chance test accuracy, but gives no exact condition. Remove V1. rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network with quadratic activation function, width N = 500
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with high weight decay; training and test curves examined.
rows.value: Both accuracies decay to random guessing after the network initially reaches 100% test accuracy and training accuracy near 100(1 − ξ)%.
rows.note: The paper attributes the later drop to weight norms collapsing. This is a case where high regularization does not preserve generalization.
rows.check: At the final endpoint both accuracies are at chance; the claimed training fit is absent. Earlier full inversion must be distinguished from later forgetting. Remove V1.

rows.measure: Training and test accuracy / qualitative phase
rows.value: Dropout enhances robustness to label corruption and facilitates better generalization; very high dropout leads to a confusion phase in which the network does not memorize all corrupted labels.
rows.note: Text gives qualitative outcomes across the phase diagram, not individual accuracy values for each plotted condition.
rows.check: This combines several distinct outcomes and should be split. Figure 19 specifies dropout 0, 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9 for coexistence, partial inversion, full inversion and confusion, respectively. Full inversion has absent corrupted-label memorization; confusion has incomplete fitting. Remove V1.

source_check.correct: Split the dropout conditions: Figure 19 identifies dropout 0.0 with coexistence, 0.3 with partial inversion, 0.6 with full inversion, and 0.9 with confusion. Corrupted-label fitting is respectively observed, partial, absent, and incomplete; one partial state cannot represent all outcomes.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network with quadratic activation function, width N = 500
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with BatchNorm and mini-batches.
rows.measure: IPR distribution and correlation between BatchNorm weights and IPR
rows.baseline: IPR distributions in the two models do not exhibit significant differences.
rows.value: BatchNorm assigns higher weights to high-IPR neurons than to low-IPR neurons; low-IPR neurons persist even in the Full Inversion phase.
rows.note: This measure describes the proposed mechanism, not training error or test error; it therefore cannot determine the accuracy behavior in V1 or V4.
rows.check: IPR distributions and BatchNorm-weight correlations measure a proposed mechanism, not training fit or test-error degradation. They cannot establish V1, V4 or V5.

rows.subject: 1-layer Transformer
